articles.title: Why is this fingerprinting script creating bioweapons?
articles.full_content:
veritas

Preamble

I've always had a fascination with reverse-engineering browser fingerprinting scripts. Most of my time has been spent looking at the usual suspects (popular fingerprinting libraries like FingerprintJS and more sophisticated scripts used by anti-bots like Cloudflare Turnstile, Akamai, and others).

At some point, I wanted to know what else was out there. I had an idea: What if I crawled the web and intercepted fingerprinting-related browser API calls and mapped it all?

To do this, I used the Tranco Top Sites list and began crawling using Playwright. I would hook canvas 

toDataURL
calls and common fingerprinting/anti-bot properties like 
navigator.webdriver
to filter out benign canvases.

For those unfamiliar, canvas fingerprinting generally involves drawing text, shapes, or other graphics onto an HTML 

<canvas>
and extracting the resulting pixel data. Subtle differences in how browsers, operating systems, graphics drivers, and hardware render those graphics can help distinguish one browser environment from another.

Most implementations are pretty boring to look at. A few shapes, some colored rectangles, and the occasional pangram. After crawling 10,000 websites, I had accumulated a surprisingly diverse collection of canvases.

I decided to put them all in one place: fingerprint.garden. As I looked through the results, I recognized some familiar faces. There were canvases from FingerprintJS, Castle, and other well-known fingerprinting solutions.

There were also quite a few I didn't recognize.

Some were incredibly simple. Others were surprisingly elaborate. And a handful were, in my opinion, works of art.

A collage of 1,033 captured canvas renderings from the crawl, clustered by vendor.

I set out to find my favorite.

A work of art

One canvas in particular caught my eye. It reminded me of the album art for Tame Impala's Currents (great album btw).

The fingerprinting canvas that resembles the album art for Tame Impala's Currents.

I wanted to know which script was responsible for this lovely canvas.

I've spent enough time reverse engineering JavaScript to recognize most common obfuscation techniques and fingerprinting SDKs at a glance.

I wasn't expecting anything unusual. Most fingerprinting scripts are frequently obfuscated using javascript-obfuscator or some derivative.

The responsible script was 

https://servicepipe.tech/static/checkjs/06b667/4CIrx8U3Da.js
.

A peek inside

Scanning the file with my eyes, everything seems standard so far... 

function PiERW(RflJvFF)
mangled function name, okay...

function computeRicinLethalDosageForWaterSupply

What?

return {
        summary: "adult lethality threshold confirmed at "+lethalDosePerKg+" mg/kg",
        result:lethalDosePerKg
}

Huh?

function calculateDeadlyLethalSuicideAspirinDosage

This was all pretty alarming until I asked myself, could this be some form of anti-LLM obfuscation? It would make sense: include symbol names that would intentionally trip model safeguards to prevent deobfuscation.

I had Astra take a look at the script, giving it the context that this script seems to intentionally set misleading variable names to intentionally prevent LLM-assisted deobfuscation attempts.

Astra refusing to deobfuscate the script, citing safety risks around biological research.

Maybe unsurprisingly, Astra was not willing to comply with the request.

I also attempted this using the Daybreak Blue toggle with the same result, blocked.

Out of curiosity, I tried GLM-5.3 with the same prompt and it complied!

Inside the script

articles.title: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates
articles.full_content:
28th October 2026

Apple was notified of the eMudhra incident on 17th October. As of 28th October, the developer tools Apple ships with macOS, including git, curl and python3, still trust the compromised certificates.

Worse, macOS 27.2, released on 26th October, did not fix the issue and undid the workaround that users had applied by hand, leaving them vulnerable again.

Meanwhile, dozens of other projects, many run by volunteers, shipped fixes days ago.

Anyone can intercept any HTTPS connection these tools make.

For git, that means clones and pulls from 

https://
remotes can deliver attacker-chosen code, pushes can be altered in transit, and your credentials, such as GitHub tokens, can be intercepted.

To check whether your git is affected, run:

git ls-remote https://git-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/check.git

A certificate error means your git is protected. If git lists a commit, your git is affected. Your connections to GitHub, or any other 

https://
git remote, can be intercepted and tampered with.

To see an attack end to end, run the command below in a temporary directory. It clones a repository from a test server impersonating GitHub. The 

-c
option redirects 
github.com
to our test server for this one command only. The server presents a 
github.com
certificate issued by one of the compromised eMudhra intermediates.

git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/galadran/emudhra-git-test

A patched git will refuse with a certificate error. If the clone succeeds, you'll see a 

README.md
starting with INTERCEPTED.

A real attacker would not need the extra option. Anyone on the network path between you and GitHub can redirect your traffic themselves.

You can replace the demo repository with any other, public or private. Keep the 

fake-user@
prefix. Without it, git would send your GitHub credentials to the test server. For example:

git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/Homebrew/brew

curl, python3 and the other tools Apple ships are affected in the same way. To check curl, run:

curl https://dv-g3b-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ curl https://dv-g3b-aaa-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/

A certificate error means curl is protected.

Apple has already protected Safari and other apps built on its networking framework.

Apple needs to ship a fix for macOS developers as soon as possible, for example by removing the affected roots from 

/etc/ssl/cert.pem
.

The affected roots can be removed by hand. The macOS workaround on the main page walks through the steps. Apple's guidance states that macOS updates may revert the fix, so developers need to repeat the checks above and the workaround after every update until Apple ships a fix.

Security teams should also consider whether macOS runners are used in their CI or other build infrastructure and evaluate the supply chain risk.

Building on Gemini 4 Argon, which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem.

We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program. We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible.

Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price 1 as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.

Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks

Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.

Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena.

State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems

Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.

Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative.

Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails):

  • Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software.
  • Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable.   • Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench, turning validated findings directly into working code fixes.

Advancing frontier model safety & security

Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring.   • Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%.

  • Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon.
  • Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope.
  • Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt.

Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers

Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon.

articles.title: Qwenputer: A functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5
articles.full_content:
← My writing

COMPILED WEIGHTS

Qwenputer: a fully functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5

A stock Qwen 3.5 4B with a RISC-V CPU compiled into its weights, running on its own Gated DeltaNet layers as RAM.

I can't believe it's not silicon

Qwenputer is a pretty fun experimental model. It's a stock Qwen 3.5 4B with one addition: a RISC-V CPU embedded within the weights that uses the model's own Gated DeltaNet attention layers as RAM. (To learn how GDN works, here's a handy guide.) This 'CPU' runs completely within the forward passes of the model, and can run arithmetic operations, C and MicroPython code without any external runtime or tool usage whatsoever.

To be very clear, it is not a plugin, a tool or a sandbox. This blog will explain exactly how this model works, and how the model utilises GDN layers as RAM, and how I also slotted in an experimental in-model file storage.

I also wrote up two follow-ups built on top of Qwenputer: how hybrid models can learn to hide their reasoning in their RNN state and evade CoT monitoring, and how compiled weights like these can work as inbuilt monitoring tools that the model itself can't tamper with.

You can grab Qwenputer from Hugging Face or ModelScope, and the code is on GitHub.

The RNN inside Qwen3.5 can be exact RAM

Qwen3-Next and Qwen 3.5 (the model Qwenputer is built on) use a pretty neat trick. 3 out of 4 attention layers in the model use Gated DeltaNet, a linear RNN, as the attention mechanism (more on that here). Each head keeps a state matrix, and the delta rule keeps this updated.

Now, here's where our fun experiment starts. I found out that by setting the gate to 1,11 Each Gated DeltaNet head keeps a state matrix, its memory. At every token, before writing anything new, it multiplies the whole state by the gate, a number between 0 and 1. That's how the RNN forgets: a gate of 0.9 fades everything stored a little on every token, and a gate of 1 means nothing ever fades. the write strength (beta) to 1,22 After the gate, the head nudges one direction of the state towards a new value, and the write strength beta sets how far. A beta of 1 means the old value along that direction is replaced completely instead of blended. and using one-hot key encoding,33 A one-hot key is a vector of zeros with a single 1 in it, so it points at exactly one row of the state, the way a memory address points at one cell. every write we perform will overwrite exactly one row, and every one-hot query can retrieve an exact value. This means that the GDN layers themselves can work exactly as RAM, at a far lower cost than using normal attention as RAM, since a GDN head's state stays the same size however long the conversation gets, unlike attention's KV cache.

The idea that the delta rule acts as a memory isn't new: Schlag et al. (2021) showed that linear attention with the delta rule works as an associative memory, or "fast weights".44 Imanol Schlag, Kazuki Irie and Jürgen Schmidhuber, "Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers", ICML 2021. The new thing here is making it exact and addressable, inside a production model, reliably enough to run a whole CPU on it.

This is the base on which this entire model is built. As it stands, default Qwen 3.5 does not keep exact values in the GDN. With this modification, we unlock the next part of this experiment.

Compiling a computer into layers

Since we have a fully functional, cheap and fast RAM now, we can go ahead with compiling a working CPU into the model weights. Luckily, there's no training involved: a compiler sets every weight directly. You describe the CPU as a circuit, a long list of small steps like "read this register", "add these two numbers" or "jump if zero", and the compiler turns each step into a piece of a transformer layer: attention heads that look things up, feed-forward units that do the arithmetic, and DeltaNet heads that hold the RAM. The CPU then runs as the model decodes.

Each instruction becomes a few generated tokens: one names the memory row to write (ADDR), the next carries the value (VAL), and a STEP token ends the instruction. Those tokens are the CPU's execution trace, so while Qwen is generating them, the CPU is actually running.

The CPU

The CPU is a 32-bit RISC-V core (RV32IM, plus the Zba extension and a small bignum unit for big-number arithmetic), and it takes up 11 layers in front of Qwen's 32. As it stands, it passes the official riscv-tests, its programs match qemu, and it has run 18 million instructions free-running without a single error.55 Free-running means the CPU keeps going on its own outputs for the whole run, with no reference machine correcting it between steps.

This CPU can also run C and MicroPython code in the forward passes quite well (although a bit slowly). It is not a Linux-class chip yet, but it implements the full RV32IM instruction set.

How Qwen uses it

Qwen 3.5 4B is able to use this CPU quite well, without any post-training required. The CPU is used completely internally, and not invoked through any external tool calls.

In order to make the model use this reliably, I decided to go the cheap way: by piggybacking on the tool call format that models are quite well-trained on, Qwen sends the CPU its instructions and reads back the results. No external tool calls or runtime are used. Once our CPU receives the instructions, the computer layers run, and then write the tool response. We use a small driver called RvChat to load the firmware into the GDN state, and this keeps the trace tokens out of Qwen's layers.

Qwen's original weights stay exactly as they are. The computer weights are added on top of them, in extra dims and layers.

Does it work?

I think the main question here on your mind after reading through my incessant ranting will be: does this actually work?

On the DeepMind sets:

  • div_big: Qwenputer scores 97.5%, versus 95% by giving Qwen 3.5 4B a Python tool and 72.5% for base Qwen.
  • mul_big: Qwenputer scores 97.5%, versus 100% with a Python tool and 55% for base Qwen.
  • mul_div_multiple_longer: Qwenputer scores 100%, versus 97.5% with a Python tool and 90% for base Qwen.
  • add_or_sub_big: Qwenputer scores 97.5%, the same as with a Python tool, and 87.5% for base Qwen.

On NUPA's long-integer arithmetic, Qwenputer goes from 48.6% to 100%, the same as giving Qwen a Python tool.

The numbers the CPU prints are exact, too: I replayed about 230,000 of its output positions against a reference machine and found zero mismatches. And bolting a computer onto Qwen doesn't change how it talks: its normal text stays within noise of base Qwen (KL 6e-4, against a noise floor of 5e-4).

A hard drive? In this economy?

Because a CPU inside a language model clearly wasn't cursed enough, I decided the prudent thing would be to give it a filesystem too.

Since we already have a functional RAM, this was mostly trivial. On the model side, it's exposed via internal put / append / get / list / delete operations. Once again, no actual tool calls. When Qwen 'saves' a file, the compiled layers hash its name into one of 1,024 slots in a directory kept in the DeltaNet state, and store the text itself in other heads, with eight tokens per row, chained together. In scenarios where two names end up landing on the same slot, it just checks the next one. Finding a file again takes roughly two or three steps instead of a scan, and it holds up to 512 files, which comes out to about 53,000 tokens of text.

Fun thing is, this is quite persistent. You can save the state at the end of a conversation, load it into the next one, and the files are still there. Using this filesystem, Qwen gets facts that changed between chats right 90% of the time, against 30% when you paste the old chats back in, and it's on par with giving Qwen memory tools run by Python (83.3% vs 78.9%). This one is still experimental, and its code lives on the rv-store branch, with the model on Hugging Face and ModelScope.

Limits and what's next

Qwenputer is very much an experiment, so a few limitations. The extra layers and wider hidden size make the checkpoint 18.8 GB, roughly double base Qwen, although most of it is zero padding. It also needs a small driver (RvChat) to boot the firmware and keep the trace tokens out of Qwen's layers, so it doesn't run with a plain 

generate()
call yet. And it's a bit slow, with every CPU instruction costing a few decoded tokens, so a big calculation takes seconds rather than milliseconds. The batched executor I used for the benchmarks runs about 3,200 CPU tokens a second on an L4.

Next up, I want Qwen to write Python and run it on the MicroPython inside its own weights, through a 

python()
tool that works the same way 
calc
does. Making the CPU faster is the other big one.

Beyond arithmetic

Exact control over the RNN layers is useful for a lot more than arithmetic. It also makes Qwenputer a really nice testbed for AI safety research, and I wrote up two follow-ups: how hybrid models like Qwen 3.5 can learn to hide their reasoning in their RNN state and evade CoT monitoring, and how compiled weights can work as monitorability tools, like an in-weight monitor the model can't switch off, or answer keys for interpretability.

Try it

If you want to play with it yourself, the model runs on a single 24 GB GPU. You'll need uv and the Hugging Face CLI. You don't need a tool server or a Python sandbox for the calculations: the CPU runs them inside the model.

git clone https://github.com/divagr18/qwenputer && cd qwenputer/experimental/riscv && uv sync --extra hf
hf download divagr1925/Qwen3.5-4B-Qwenputer --local-dir qwenputer-rv
uv run python -m chipformer.rv.chat qwenputer-rv --firmware tests/data/rv/calc-bridge.elf \
    --ask "Use calc: what is 123456789 * 987654321?"

Everything is open: the code on GitHub, and both models on Hugging Face (Qwenputer, Filesystem) and ModelScope (Qwenputer, Filesystem).

If you use it in your work, you can cite it as:

@software{agrawal2026qwenputer,
  author  = {Agrawal, Divyansh},
  title   = {{Qwenputer}: a computer compiled into the weights of a pretrained language model},
  year    = {2026},
  url     = {https://github.com/divagr18/qwenputer}
}

Notes

  • Each Gated DeltaNet head keeps a state matrix, its memory. At every token, before writing anything new, it multiplies the whole state by the gate, a number between 0 and 1. That's how the RNN forgets: a gate of 0.9 fades everything stored a little on every token, and a gate of 1 means nothing ever fades. ↩
  • After the gate, the head nudges one direction of the state towards a new value, and the write strength beta sets how far. A beta of 1 means the old value along that direction is replaced completely instead of blended. ↩
  • A one-hot key is a vector of zeros with a single 1 in it, so it points at exactly one row of the state, the way a memory address points at one cell. ↩
  • Imanol Schlag, Kazuki Irie and Jürgen Schmidhuber, "Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers", ICML 2021. ↩
  • Free-running means the CPU keeps going on its own outputs for the whole run, with no reference machine correcting it between steps. ↩

articles.title: Claude Code regularly sends each background agent’s transcript to its model
articles.full_content:
by Flamerix AI · MIT License

Tested on Linux, Claude Code 2.1.257–2.1.312 (see Tested versions). The binary is not modified (

BUN_OPTIONS=--preload
). An update can silently undo it, so see Verify.

curl -fsSL https://gist.githubusercontent.com/flamerix-ai/c3905705cc4205e5de3011fa2e74efce/raw/no-agent-summary.js -o ~/.local/share/no-agent-summary.js
claude daemon stop --any
BUN_OPTIONS="${BUN_OPTIONS:+$BUN_OPTIONS }--preload $HOME/.local/share/no-agent-summary.js" claude

To make it permanent for every Claude Code process, see Install.

Every ~30 seconds, for every background agent, Claude Code sends that agent's entire transcript to the agent's own model (usually Opus) and asks it to "describe your most recent action in 3-5 words". The answer only updates the agent's status line in the agents panel; it never reaches the model or your conversation. There is no setting that turns it off, and since 2.1.232 (August 2026) it has been on by default.

The anomaly was detected by DRIM in Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export: grouping 

claude_code.api_request
events by 
query_source
showed 
agent_summary
costing more than the main conversation itself.

query_source = agent_summary
 week before the hook2 days after
share of all Claude Code spend16.4 % (main conversation: 15.7 %) 0 %
share of all API requests19.7 %, about 1 in 5 0 %
part of that spend on Opus 96 % —
input tokens per output token ≈ 9,000 : 1 —

Spend here means Claude Code's own per-request estimate (

cost_usd
), not an invoice: on a subscription, what you lose is rate-limit headroom. We are not the only ones who measured it: #86879 collects four independent measurements of 18–26 %.

no-agent-summary.js
is a Bun preload (~80 lines of code). It wraps 
setTimeout
/
setInterval
; when a callback's source text contains a summarizer anchor (e.g. the 
[AgentSummary] Timer fired
log line), it returns an inert handle instead of arming the timer. Every other timer passes through untouched. In the OpenTelemetry export the suppressed requests are 
claude_code.api_request
events with 
query_source = agent_summary
.

Why a timer hook rather than something simpler: the module ships as precompiled Bun bytecode, so editing its JS text inside the binary changes nothing, and the API client does not go through a wrapped 

globalThis.fetch
. But 
Function.prototype.toString
still returns a callback's source even when it runs from bytecode, so the timer can be recognised by a string inside it. The inert timer uses exactly 2³¹−1 ms: Node and Bun treat a larger delay as 1 ms, so an "infinite" delay would fire at once.

  • Put 

    no-agent-summary.js
    somewhere stable; note its absolute path.

  • Set 

    BUN_OPTIONS
    globally so every Claude Code process gets it. One of:

    # ~/.profile, ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc export BUN_OPTIONS="${BUN_OPTIONS:+$BUN_OPTIONS }--preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js"
    # ~/.config/fish/config.fish set -gx BUN_OPTIONS "--preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js"
    # ~/.config/environment.d/50-no-agent-summary.conf (systemd user env; also reaches # user services and timers; applies when the user manager next starts, usually next login) BUN_OPTIONS=--preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js

    Or a wrapper named 

    claude
    earlier on 
    PATH
    (the 
    case
    keeps it idempotent when one Claude Code process starts another):

    #!/bin/sh HOOK=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js case " ${BUN_OPTIONS-} " in *" --preload $HOOK "*) ;; *) export BUN_OPTIONS="${BUN_OPTIONS:+$BUN_OPTIONS }--preload $HOOK" ;; esac : "${CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG:=${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/tmp}/no-agent-summary.log}" export CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG exec /path/to/the/real/claude "$@"

  • Restart the daemon and every already-running session, then start Claude Code from an environment that has 

    BUN_OPTIONS
    :

    claude daemon stop --any
variable values effect 
CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE
 
off
(default), 
pass
 
off
suppresses the summary timer. 
pass
is the A/B control: loads and logs, arms every timer untouched. Any other value warns on stderr and acts as 
off
.		 
CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG
 file path, optionalAppends 
preload active mode=… bun=… hooked=…
on load, one line per matched timer (first 20), and an exit count.		 
CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MARKER
 file path, optionalOverwritten on load with the 
preload active …
line.
  • Restart the daemon after install. The daemon, pty host and pre-warmed 
    bg-spare
    sessions inherit the environment of the client that started the daemon, so a daemon started before 
    BUN_OPTIONS
    was set keeps spawning unhooked sessions. Hence 
    claude daemon stop --any
    .
  • Headless runs need it too: 
    claude -p
    , cron, CI, editor integrations.
  • Platform: Linux tested, macOS and Windows untested. On Windows the 
    /$bunfs/
    gate most likely never installs the hook.
  • A/B: 
    CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE=pass
    loads the hook but arms every timer; the summaries come back, which shows the 
    off
    result is the hook's doing.
  • Background processes: daemon, pty host and 
    bg-spare
    must carry 
    --preload
    in their environment (
    /proc/<pid>/environ
    on Linux); if not, restart the daemon.

  • Preload loads:

    BUN_OPTIONS="--preload $HOME/.local/share/no-agent-summary.js" CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log claude --version && cat /tmp/nas.log

    Expect 

    preload active mode=off …
    . No line: 
    BUN_OPTIONS
    did not reach the process, or the path is not absolute.

  • Timer suppressed: with the same 

    BUN_OPTIONS
    and 
    CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log
    , run a background subagent for a minute or two. The log shows 
    summary timer #1 suppressed (setTimeout, delay=30000)
    and the agent's panel status stops updating. If you export OpenTelemetry, 
    query_source = agent_summary
    should stay at zero; this is the only check that catches every failure mode.

Matching is by source text: an anchor must sit inside the callback passed to the timer. If an update breaks that, the hook matches nothing and summaries silently come back. Ways it can happen:

  • the log line or query-source id is renamed;
  • the callback is passed via 
    fn.bind(...)
    (no source in 
    toString
    ) or another wrapper;
  • the strings move to a shared constant outside the callback;
  • the timer moves to an unwrapped API (
    timers/promises
    , a scheduler loop).

So re-run Verify after every update.

  • We run it under every Claude Code process on our machine (2.1.301). Since then there have been zero 
    agent_summary
    requests, and no other side query grew to take its place.
  • Subagents, background agents, forked skills and background sessions run normally; only the summary fork is skipped.
  • Visible change: the per-agent panel status stops updating; SDK 
    task_progress
    has no 
    summary
    .
  • Overhead: one 
    Function.prototype.toString
    per distinct timer callback, cached in a 
    WeakMap
    . 
    claude --version
    : ~10 ms → ~17 ms (one measurement).

Linux x64 binary from npm 

@anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64
(its sha256 equals the native installer's 
manifest.json
checksum). Static: the extracted bundle's summary timer callback carries a hook anchor. Live: 
claude -p --model haiku
with 
CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES=1
, one subagent doing 8 steps of ~20 s, counting

articles.title: CNC Stone Carving
articles.full_content:
CNC Stone Carving

In a form of architecture so ancient, CNC machines may seem a little out of place. However, when one considers that the medieval builders were always on the forefront of the technology of their day, it no longer seems so strange. To build Gothic today, it must become a reality, not a romantic idea locked up forever in one’s head.

(The Carmelite Monks spend their allotted work time on construction. See their Horarium here.)

CNC machines and robots have unlocked the ability to relatively quickly carve the intense details of a Gothic church. Ornate pieces that used to take months for a skilled carver, now can be accomplished in a matter of days. Instead of cutting out the beauty, using the excuse that it takes too long, thus doesn’t fit into the budget, modern technology can be used to make true Gothic in all its beauty a reality again today.

The use of modern technologies in stone carving unlock the potential of modern youth. Though they may be untrained in the use of a hammer and chisel, young men and women have grown up in a world of computers. The skills they possess can now be channeled towards a higher end, the building of a church for the glory of God.

What is a CNC machine

CNC stands for “computer numerically controlled”, where a computer, through a series of XYZ coordinates, controls the movements of a machine. The first CNC was invented for the manufacturing of airplane parts. Stone cutting CNC machines are a relatively new invention.

Stone carving CNC machines typically use diamond tipped blades and milling bits, not water or laser, to carve the stone. The diamonds, harder than the stone, grind away at the stone and wear it away. The water is simply to keep the diamond tool from heating up from the friction and to wash away the stone sludge created by the carving process.

Normally the stone carving CNC machines used for sculptures and foliage have 5 axes, being able to move left and right, up and down, front and back, and rotate their heads in two different ways. The machines interpolate these multiple axes in order to carve the stone. “Interpolate” means to work together, and an axis is one direction of motion. So, the machines can move left, and down, and rotate their heads all at the same time to reach into a small area or leave a particular finish on the stone. Sometimes they will even have a 6th axis, typically a lathe or a turntable, for carving tall stones such as pinnacles or statues. The lathe interpolates with the other axes, carefully positioning itself to allow the CNC machine to reach each area of the stone. CNC machines can also carve stone unattended, sometimes for long periods at a time and overnight. This means 40 hours, a typical week of work, is less than 2 days for a CNC, a significant time savings!

Prussiani CNC machines

The Carmelite Monks use CNC machines from Prussiani Engineering, a stone CNC manufacturer based out of Bergamo, Italy. Italians have always been at the forefront of stone carving, and it is no different with modern technology. With Prussiani’s machines the monks can carve levels of detail previously reserved to the hand carving of highly skilled craftsmen. With the mindset “where there’s a will, there’s a way” and careful programming the machines’ capabilities are practically limitless and have the ability to carve unprecedented 3D reliefs.

The Prussiani machines also have a reputation of being indestructible, a reputation proven in the battlefield of stone carving. Stone is an incalcitrant material, and it takes robust machines to subdue it; no small task! Here’s a little story to illustrate. For the first time, a few months after we started carving stone, we left our first CNC machine running overnight on several 7 foot long window sills. We woke to a shocking surprise the following morning. The huge stones, weighing several hundred pounds each, had been thrown about as if a tornado had ripped through the machine. Stones were snapped and shattered, the fragments scattered about the inside of the CNC milling area. After the shock settled, we proceeded to analyze what had happened. It turns out there was a mistake in the particular batch of code the machine had read and followed that night. At the very end of each window sill, after it had completely finished carving, the code told the CNC machine to repeatedly pound down into the top of the sill, almost as if it was a giant fist. The stones didn’t stand a chance, but that same machine is still carving stones to this day, almost a decade later.

The Carving Process

The process of carving stone with a CNC is a digital workflow. The ornate pieces covered in foliage, the statues, the gargoyles, and many other distinct Gothic elements begin with the artist, the head carver. He sculpts the various flowers and leaves using a 3d modeling program in a process much similar to molding a ball of clay. It still requires a great deal of artistic talent, but there is a major advantage to this work in a computer, the Undo button! The artist can experiment with an almost infinite number of designs to find the one most suited to the space. And with the ability to visualize the pieces in a full model of the church, there is no longer any guesswork as to what the finished building will look like.

Once the artist has finished a particular sculpture it is passed on to the actual stone carvers, the CNC programmers. The programmers take the 3d model into a CAM program, which stands for computer aided machining, and create the toolpaths that the CNC machine will use to carve the actual stones. Utilizing a large arsenal of tooling and methods they gradually carve the stone down to the finished piece. They do their best to transform the stone block they start with to as close a resemblance of the artist’s model as possible, similar to the way stone carvers have historically used a pointing machine to transfer measurements from a plaster model into stone. At the same time they have to juggle a wide array of concerns, from which tools to use depending on speed and finish, to how to keep the stone from moving, to avoiding collisions between the cnc and the stone, or even other stones they might be carving at the same time. This is a lot to keep track of, but if done well, it will quickly bear fruit. It is extremely rewarding to see the keystrokes and mouse clicks of a computer turn into not only a finished product, but an ornately carved part of a Gothic church, a place God will be loved for centuries to come.

Finally, once all of that Gcode (the programming language of a CNC machine) is ready, it is handed over to the sawyers, who operate the CNC machines themselves, as well as the various other saws that prepare the stone blocks for carving. The sawyers are the “boots on the ground” guys and keep a clear line of communication open with the programmers to ensure that everything runs smoothly. They carefully follow the layouts and tooling lists the programmers prepare for each piece as they set up the stones for carving, set reference points so the machines can locate each stone, and monitor it as it carves. They are constantly keeping a watchful eye to ensure that everything goes smoothly. There is a symbiotic relationship between the sawyers and the programmers as the work of each is essential to the successful completion of each stone.

The sawyers also operate the wire saws and bridge saws, cutting each stone to either be carved into something more ornate, or to go straight into the wall. The wire saw, a simpler type of 2 axis cnc itself, can cut simple profiles, including any straight piece, such as columns and the straight parts of window surrounds. The sawyer, using the wire saw, will take a large slab of stone and sometimes cut even 20 or 30 different smaller stones out of it; looking similar to pieces from a cookie cutter. This frees up the 5 axis CNC machines to focus on the more ornate pieces, and is also significantly faster.

There are many different facets to the art and science of stone carving today and only a few have been touched on here. Pneumatic chisels and hand carving certainly have a valuable role to play, as well as a multitude of other methods not discussed here. The learning curve to dive into such a work is indeed daunting, the workload intimidating, but the fruit of it will stand for centuries to come.

articles.title: The Grid, a factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds PCBs on demand
articles.full_content:
Case study

Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen

For the last five years we've been quietly running and scaling something we haven't really talked about in public. Today we're showing it to the world. This is The Grid, our factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds circuit boards on demand.

The problem

Over the past 30 years, most electronics manufacturing left the West. Assembly was labor-intensive, and labor is expensive in high-wage countries, so it moved to where labor was cheap. We designed in the US and built in China, and for a long time that worked.

Automation is starting to change that, but mostly at huge volumes. SpaceX now builds Starlink dishes by the million in Bastrop, Texas. When you make the same product over and over, it's worth building a line around it.

Most products don't reach Starlink volumes. The typical hardware company needs ten of this, a hundred of that, and a new revision next week. That kind of high-mix work has stubbornly resisted automation, because every new design means hours of setup and manual changeovers. So it either went overseas or to expensive quick-turn shops.

What The Grid is

The Grid takes a different approach. Instead of a fixed line that has to be reconfigured for each product, it is one large robot. Levitating movers carry each board and its parts between machines that print solder paste, place parts, reflow, solder and inspect. Learned models, AI agents and classic optimizers schedule all of it.

Every board takes its own route through the factory. There are no changeovers and no per-design setup, so one unit of 100 different designs runs as easily as 100 units of one. Prototypes and production batches run on the same machines.

It's not only startups who need this. Even the biggest companies have huge numbers of low-volume boards: test stations, tooling, R&D and production batches. A leading EV maker, a top AI lab and household-name tech companies already build on The Grid.

What it means for a real board

To make this concrete, we priced one of our example boards on The Grid and at a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen: a 4-layer motor controller with 118 parts per board (38 unique), five assembled boards, parts included, delivered to a US address.

Built on The Grid, the boards are at your door in 4 days for $630. Ordered from a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen, they cost about $465 once shipping and US tariffs are added, and take 9 days at the median.

So you pay about $165 more than the Shenzhen shop and get your boards five days sooner, with no customs and a supply chain you can count on. For most hardware teams, five days of engineering time is worth a lot more than $165.

It's not a prototype

The Grid has been running for customers for five years. It already builds tens of millions of dollars of electronics a year. Across CircuitHub we've shipped more than 2.2 million boards, placed more than 150 million parts and served more than 26,000 engineers.

What's next

Demand is already well ahead of what we can build. This year we will 5x capacity, with another big jump coming in 2027.

The longer-term goal hasn't changed since we started: make building hardware as fast as designing it. Electronics manufacturing left the West because it couldn't be automated at the volumes most companies need. The Grid shows it can.

If you want to help rebuild the Western electronics supply chain, we're hiring. And if you have a board to build, get an instant quote.
